race_context: The School City of Whiting serves the city of Whiting in Lake County {wiki_scw}. It runs three schools: Nathan Hale Elementary School, Whiting Middle School and Whiting High School {wiki_scw}. Federal data list 1,091 students in grades pre-K through 12 and 64 full-time-equivalent classroom teachers, drawn from the 2024-25 and 2025-26 school years {nces_scw}.

Superintendent: Lake County's public officials directory, dated Aug. 13, 2026, lists Cynthia Scroggins {lc_directory}. Wikipedia's entry on the district lists David Verta, citing the district's staff page {wiki_scw}. This guide could not load the district website to confirm who leads the district now.

The board has five members, all elected at large {lc_directory}. The terms of Patricia Herbst and Christopher R. Davenport expire Dec. 31, 2026; Bruce Stolman, Rena Mindas and Jonathan (TJ) Toth serve terms through Dec. 31, 2028 {lc_directory}.

Seats on the 2026 ballot: two at-large seats, not one as the state list shows {in_list}. Lake County's sample ballot tells Whiting voters to 'Vote for not more than Two (2)' in the School City of Whiting At Large race, and the county's results page also lists the race as vote for 2 {lc_sample_w01}{lc_results_2026}. Both incumbents filed again, Herbst on June 1 and Davenport on June 10, 2026, and they are the only two candidates {lc_candidates}{lc_sample_w01}. The ballot lists Herbst as 'Democratic Party' and Davenport as 'Independent' {lc_sample_w01}.
2022 results for these seats: in a vote-for-2 race, Davenport received 46.63% of the vote and Herbst 30.44%, defeating Stephanie Madison (22.92%) {lc_results_2022}.

Seats not on this ballot: in 2024 voters chose three members from five candidates; Jonathan (Tj) Toth (28.28%), Rena Mindas (25.23%) and Thomas Ehrlich (21.28%) finished in the top three {lc_results_2024}. The 2026 county directory lists Bruce Stolman, not Ehrlich, in one of the terms ending in 2028 {lc_directory}; this guide did not find how that seat changed hands.

Operating referendum (Nov. 3, 2026, Public Question #3): the board adopted a resolution on June 1, 2026 finding that, under current revenue projections for 2027 through 2034, the district 'will not be able to carry out its public educational duty' without a referendum levy {dlgf_op_res_2026}. The question asks voters to approve a property-tax rate of up to $0.3372 per $100 of assessed value for up to eight years, raising no more than $2,500,000 a year; the state says this would raise the tax bill on a $250,000 median home by $383 a year {dlgf_op_2026}{lc_sample_w01}. The ballot language gives the purposes as responding to 'reductions in property tax revenue,' keeping school resource officers, attracting and retaining teachers and staff, maintaining class sizes and funding academic and student support programs {dlgf_op_2026}.

The district's revenue spending plan estimates $2.5 million from the levy in 2027 and would spend it on retaining teachers and staff ($1,250,000), student health and safety ($527,098), maintaining class sizes ($344,111) and academic programs ($378,791) {dlgf_op_plan_2026}. The board's resolution says no charter school asked in writing to share in the levy, so none is planned {dlgf_op_res_2026}.

Capital referendum (Nov. 3, 2026, Public Question #4): the district is also asking voters to approve up to $39,305,000 in borrowing, plus up to $28,810,000 in interest and fees, over no more than 23 years, for its '2026 Student Facilities, Safety, and Transportation Improvement Project' {dlgf_cp_2026}{lc_sample_w01}. The project includes security upgrades at all schools, renovations and possible additions at all school buildings, technology-ready classrooms, athletic, support, performing arts and music facilities including a band room, and equipment, technology and buses {dlgf_cp_2026}. The tax increase is capped at $3,500,000 a year, or $530 a year on a $250,000 median home {dlgf_cp_2026}. The board adopted its preliminary resolution on the project June 1, 2026, and the Lake County election board approved the ballot language June 16 {lc_cp_res_2026}.

Earlier referendum: in November 2023, Whiting voters rejected an eight-year operating referendum at a rate of $0.17 per $100 of assessed value {dlgf_op_2023}{dlgf_hist}{wfyi_ref_2023}. According to WFYI, the district estimated that legislative changes had cost it more than $3 million since 2018, and its website said that without the money class sizes would increase and the district would lose teachers {wfyi_lake_2023}.
Forums: this guide found no candidate forums, questionnaires or news coverage of the 2026 Whiting school board race. With two candidates for two seats, the race is uncontested {lc_sample_w01}.

candidates.summary: Incumbent; listed in the county directory as Christopher R. Davenport, with a term ending Dec. 31, 2026 {lc_directory}. He is one of two candidates for two at-large seats {lc_sample_w01}.
background: Is a current member of the Whiting school board {lc_directory}. Occupation, community roles and any ties to the schools were not found.
path_to_ballot: Filed June 10, 2026 and is listed on the ballot as 'Independent' {lc_candidates}{lc_sample_w01}{in_list}.
Won the seat in 2022 with 46.63% of the vote, the highest share in a vote-for-2 race {lc_results_2022}.
on_incumbent: Is a current board member {lc_directory}. No public statements by him about the board's record were found.
gaps: No news coverage, candidate forum or questionnaire responses, campaign website, social-media page, endorsements or campaign finance reports were found for this candidate. The School City of Whiting website (whiting.k12.in.us) blocked automated access, and The Times of Northwest Indiana (nwitimes.com) is behind a paid gateway, so neither could be read for this guide.
Occupation, community roles and any ties to the schools not found.
His position on the two 2026 district referendums was not found; as a board member he serves on the board that adopted the referendum resolutions, but the vote tally on them was not found.
